clue.text: TV team's working with painter whose oeuvre isn't in a gallery

definitions.text: whose oeuvre isn't in a gallery
definitions.note: a relative clause, not a noun: it leans on painter, which does double duty as anagram letters and as the noun it describes

indicators.note: a team that is working is busy and moving about, so these letters are rearranged into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, with the S of the possessive
taken as written; the same word is also the noun the definition describes

explanation.surface: A television crew is filming an artist whose work never hangs in any gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: The word painter does double duty: its letters join the anagram and it also heads the definition. A pavement artist chalks pictures on the street for passing coins.
explanation.definitionFit: Street artists draw in chalk on paving stones outdoors, so their work is seen on the ground rather than displayed on gallery walls.

clue.text: Frequently, agitator restrained by braces as they are

definitions.text: Frequently, agitator restrained by braces as they are

indicators.note: something restrained is held in on both sides, so the earlier words sit inside the word that follows

parts.note: a brace is a pair, so braces are pairs; this wraps around the rest
oft is an old word for often
someone who rouses or stirs up a crowd

explanation.surface: A troublemaker is held in check by some sort of braces, as such people often are.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a whole, the clue describes the answer: trousers are often held up by braces, the British word for suspenders.
explanation.definitionFit: Trousers are commonly kept up by shoulder straps, so the full clue is a description of the garment it builds.

clue.text: Be seen no more as a vehicle?

parts.note: a van is a road vehicle
the suffix -ish means like or in the manner of

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether to disappear by pretending to be a car or lorry.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful reading: something van-ish is like a van. Note the parts come in reverse clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: To vanish is to disappear from sight, so it means to stop being seen.

clue.text: Is traitor up to tech firm's five pieces afoot?

parts.note: Meta is the company that owns Facebook

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from the bottom to the top

parts.note: taken as written
a rat is someone who betrays their side

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a traitor is busy plotting against a big tech company.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversed part comes after the firm in the answer, even though it opens the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The metatarsals are the five long bones in each foot, between the ankle and the toes.

clue.text: Yielding sinners not at fault

indicators.note: something at fault has gone wrong, so the letters are in the wrong order and must be rearranged

parts.note: the twelve letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Those who give way to temptation are not really to blame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At fault' seems to finish a moral statement about sinners, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who offers no opposition gives way readily, which is what yielding means.

clue.text: See 1
Right oven for this?

parts.note: R is the standard abbreviation for right
an oast is a kiln for drying hops

explanation.surface: A cook wonders whether this is the correct oven for the dish.
explanation.walkthrough: An oast is a kiln for drying hops, a common sight in Kent with its cone roof. Read as a whole, the clue asks what you would cook in an oven.
explanation.definitionFit: A joint of meat cooked in the oven is a roast, so the right oven is the place for one.

clue.text: Many an investigation isn't planned to cover queues abandoned by the centre

indicators.note: to cover something is to go around it, so one part wraps the other
something planned is arranged, so these letters are set in a new arrangement

parts.note: the four letters to be rearranged, around the other part

indicators.note: being abandoned by the centre means losing the letters in the middle of the word

parts.note: taken as written, before its centre is removed

explanation.surface: An investigation that wasn't planned has to deal with queues that people have left.
explanation.walkthrough: The centre of a six-letter word is its middle two letters. 'Planned' could seem to describe the investigation, but it works on the apostrophe-free letters of isn't.
explanation.definitionFit: An inquest is a judicial inquiry into a death, so inquests are a plural for many investigations.

clue.text: He or she print data, not as planned for him or her

indicators.note: something planned is arranged, so these letters are set in a new order
as is read as the plural of the letter A, so the instruction is to leave out every A

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written, before its vowels go

explanation.surface: Someone printing data finds it does not turn out as intended for a particular person.
explanation.walkthrough: DATA without its two As leaves DT. 'He or she' looks like the definition, but it is part of the anagram, and the definition is 'him or her' at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar, he, she, him and her are pronouns of the third person, the one spoken about.

clue.text: Two gins and it mixed for setting off

indicators.note: drinks that are mixed are stirred together, so these letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: the word gin twice
taken as written

explanation.surface: A barman combines a double gin and something else to get a party started.
explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords 'it' often means Italian vermouth, as in gin and it, but here it is just two letters in the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Igniting something sets it alight, and setting off a firework or explosion is lighting it.

clue.text: Make short tent

indicators.note: something short is cut down, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a marquee is a large tent used at weddings and fairs

explanation.surface: An instruction to put up a small tent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make' looks like a verb but is the noun, as in the make of a car.
explanation.definitionFit: A marque is a brand of car or other vehicle, which is what the noun make means.

clue.text: Encourages Sherlock of late to get breakfast

parts.note: to egg someone on is to urge them
Benedict Cumberbatch played Sherlock Holmes in the recent BBC series

explanation.surface: Someone urges the detective to go and have his morning meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sherlock of late' means the most recent screen Sherlock, Benedict Cumberbatch in the BBC's Sherlock.
explanation.definitionFit: Poached eggs and ham on a muffin with hollandaise sauce is a classic brunch or morning dish.

clue.text: Start of Macron's ethnocentrism

indicators.note: of here means taken from, so the letters are drawn from within the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A comment on how the French president's nationalism began.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start of' looks like an instruction to take a first letter, but Start is the definition and the answer straddles the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: The onset of something is its beginning, as in the onset of winter.

clue.text: Draw in height, first to last, for 1.25%

indicators.note: in means one part is placed inside the other
the opening letter is moved to the end of the word, leaving the rest in order

parts.note: taken as written, before its first letter moves
a drawn match is a tie

explanation.surface: Instructions for sketching a figure at a set height in a technical drawing.
explanation.walkthrough: The cycled word is itself a fraction, one eighth, and the drawn match sits inside it to make the answer, a much smaller fraction.
explanation.definitionFit: One part in eighty is 1/80, which as a percentage is 1.25 per cent.

clue.text: Geeky type teaches at Hogwarts?

parts.note: to train someone is to teach them
Harry Potter is the pupil taught at Hogwarts, the wizarding school

explanation.surface: A nerdy person works as a teacher at Harry Potter's school of magic.
explanation.walkthrough: A teacher at Hogwarts trains Potter. A trainspotter, in Britain, is a hobbyist who logs locomotive numbers, a byword for a nerd.
explanation.definitionFit: Trainspotters collect railway engine numbers, a hobby that made the word slang for an obsessive enthusiast.

clue.text: Exposed bottom to secure trick

parts.note: overt means open, done in plain view
the rump is the backside

explanation.surface: Someone bares their backside to pull off a prank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trick' suggests a prank, but it is the card-game sense.
explanation.definitionFit: In card games like whist and bridge, playing a higher trump than one already played wins the trick for you.

clue.text: See 1
Four articles about totalitarianism's ultimate bête noire

indicators.note: about means going around, so the little words sit around the single letter

parts.note: the articles an, a, the and a

indicators.note: ultimate means final, so only the last letter of the word is used

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Newspaper pieces discussing the ultimate evil of totalitarianism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' suggests newspaper pieces, but means the grammatical articles an, a and the.
explanation.definitionFit: Anathema is something intensely loathed, which is what a bête noire, French for black beast, is.

clue.text: Neophiliac's line may be winning there

indicators.note: may be suggests a possible other form, so the letters could be reordered into something else

parts.note: the twelve letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A lover of novelty's approach could be a successful one.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase comes from Tennyson's 'Ring out the old, ring in the new', used to welcome the New Year.
explanation.definitionFit: A neophiliac loves novelty, so welcoming fresh things is the kind of phrase such a person would say.

clue.text: Escort for concert top solo

indicators.note: to top something is to cut off its head, so the word loses its first letter

parts.note: a gig is a live music performance
taken as written, before its head is removed

explanation.surface: A musician seeks a companion for a gig, or plays the best solo there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top solo' reads as the best solo, but top is a verb meaning remove the head.
explanation.definitionFit: A gigolo is a man paid to accompany women, which is one sense of an escort.

clue.text: See 8
Absolute pittance left by ex-PM's declaration

parts.note: utter means complete, absolute

indicators.note: what is left by someone is what remains when they go away, so that name is removed

parts.note: taken as written, before the name is removed
William Pitt, father and son, were British Prime Ministers

explanation.surface: A former prime minister announces that some sum is utterly paltry.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing PITT from PITTANCE leaves ANCE; Pitt the Elder and Pitt the Younger were both 18th-century British Prime Ministers.
explanation.definitionFit: An utterance is something said aloud, a spoken statement, which a declaration is.

clue.text: Fruit farm starts out in mountains

indicators.note: with the starts out, each word loses its first letter

parts.note: an orange is a citrus fruit
a grange is a farmhouse with its farm buildings

explanation.surface: Someone sets up an orchard business high in the hills.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words lose their first letter and both leave the same five letters, so either one alone gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A range is a line or chain of mountains, as in the Pennine range.

clue.text: Yours in slime?

parts.note: the whole word, which must be read in two parts as the next blocks show
the first four letters of slime, read as a word meaning slender
the last letter of slime, taken as written

explanation.surface: A letter signed off in some disgusting goo.
explanation.walkthrough: The trick is to split slime into two parts, an adjective and a lone letter. The question mark warns that the word must be broken up.
explanation.definitionFit: Thine is the old possessive form of thou, meaning belonging to you.

clue.text: They leave next generation outside the European Union

indicators.note: outside means going around, so the rearranged letters wrap the other part
generation means creating something, so a new word is produced from these letters

parts.note: the four letters to be rearranged
EU is the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Young people are leaving the EU behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Next generation' reads as one phrase about young people, but generation is the anagram signal for next.
explanation.definitionFit: Exeunt is the stage direction, Latin for they go out, telling several actors to leave the stage.

clue.text: Drunk and unfussy lover you picked up wearing cropped top

indicators.note: something wearing a garment is inside it, so that garment goes around the letter
cropped means cut short, so the garment loses its final letter

parts.note: short for bisexual, someone not fussy about the sex of a partner
a blouse is a top worn by women

indicators.note: something picked up is heard, so the word is identified by its sound

parts.note: the letter U sounds like the word

explanation.surface: A tipsy, easy-going partner in a midriff-baring top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cropped top' looks like a midriff-baring garment, but cropped is an instruction to cut the word short. Bi is informal for bisexual.
explanation.definitionFit: Bibulous means fond of drinking alcohol, which describes someone who is often drunk.

clue.text: Christian vibrator

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a member of an American religious sect known for plain living and furniture
second meaning: something that is shaken or that shakes

explanation.walkthrough: The pairing is meant to raise an eyebrow; the vibrator is a cocktail shaker or salt shaker.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shakers were a religious community named for their trembling in worship, and a shaker is any device that shakes.

clue.text: Quit rejecting cat and dog and budgie cover

indicators.note: to reject is to throw back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: cats and dogs are household pets
down is the soft feathers covering a bird such as a budgerigar

explanation.surface: Someone gives up their animals and even the cloth over the birdcage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Budgie cover' suggests the cloth over a birdcage at night, but means the bird's own feathers.
explanation.definitionFit: To step down is to resign from a post, which is one sense of the verb quit.
